title: New apartments, townhomes get green light from Plano commission
text:
Markdown Content:
Plano residents could see additional housing developments coming to south Plano.

At their March 2 [meeting](https://planotx.new.swagit.com/videos/376735), Plano Planning and Zoning commissioners approved a request to amend the development standards for the Heritage Creekside urban mixed-use district. The changes allow additional residential housing, retail and commercial uses within the development.

**What you need to know**

[Heritage Creekside](https://content.civicplus.com/api/assets/tx-plano/869dbced-815f-4c1d-bab5-c50bdd804fcd) is a 156-acre mixed-use development located at the intersection of Plano Parkway and Alma Drive. The mixed-use district was established in 2014, and development plans have been modified several times since then, according to meeting documents.

At full build-out, the development is expected to include 2,342 residential units, according to the property’s [website](https://theretailconnection.net/wp-content/uploads/2025/06/Plano-TX-Heritage-Creekside_02.16.26-Reduced.pdf).

The previous plan for about 37 acres of undeveloped land included a mix of six-to-25-story offices, one-to-two-story retail and office buildings, and four-to-15-story hotels. However, city documents state that plan was “no longer economically viable as originally envisioned.”

Developer Rosewood Property Co. requested several changes to the district, including:

*   Expanding the district by rezoning 4.1 acres from light industrial to urban mixed-use to add townhomes
*   Modifying the required mix of uses to allow more residential and retail
*   Allowing outdoor commercial amusement uses, such as game courts, table games and mini golf
*   Allowing additional multifamily and single-family residential units with certain parts of the development

**Breaking it down**

Under the approved plan, the development would include a total of 342 single-family residential units and 2,000 multifamily units at full build-out, according to [city documents](https://content.civicplus.com/api/assets/tx-plano/869dbced-815f-4c1d-bab5-c50bdd804fcd).

Plano Lead Planner Molly Coryell said the proposal had previously been tabled in January to allow the developer to incorporate a phasing plan, tying the nonresidential development to the additional multifamily units.

At least 12,000 square feet of new, nonresidential development must be completed before issuing new multifamily permits and construction on certain parts of the property, according to city documents.

**Zooming in**

Coryell said city staff supported the 4.1-acre expansion, but they recommended denying the broader changes to the urban mixed-use district because they conflict with Plano’s comprehensive plan.

Coryell added the history of zoning changes for the property indicate the property is evolving into a high-density neighborhood rather than a mixed-use district.

“We think it becomes mostly a residential district, not a mixed-use district,” Assistant Planning Director Michael Bell said.

According to city documents, the plan is inconsistent with the city’s comprehensive plan and does not align with the intent of the urban mixed-use district or future land use category.

**What they’re saying**

Bill Dahlstrom, representative for Rosewood, said the development will be high-quality and the company plans to invest in Plano for the long-term.1

He noted staff’s concerns about the mix of uses in the development, adding that “in today’s world, those just don’t work, and they’re not going to work.”

“It has been ... a legacy development for the city, and that’s what we want to continue,” Dahlstrom said. “We think we came up with a phasing plan that works for us all.”

Commissioner Michael Brounoff voted against the request, saying he wanted stronger commitments from the developer on future nonresidential uses in the development, such as with the office space.

title: Eastside apartment expansion underway in Richardson
text:
Markdown Content:
Construction is underway on an expansion to the [Eastside apartment complex](https://www.maac.com/texas/dallas/maa-eastside/), which is located near North Central Expressway and Campbell Road in Richardson.

A groundbreaking ceremony was held March 9 for the development, known as The Caroline Eastside, which is located at 1735 N. Greenville Ave. adjacent to sister property The Mallory Eastside. The Caroline will include 384 apartment units with a mix of studio, one-, two- and three-bedroom options, according to a [press release](https://www.prnewswire.com/news-releases/hunt-companies-to-develop-luxury-multifamily-project---the-caroline-eastside-apartments-in-richardson-tx-301771969.html).

"The Caroline will provide ideally located, modern Class-A residences to support the growing demand for multifamily housing in Richardson,” said Ben Wullschlager, senior vice president of Hunt, in a statement.

Apartment amenities include spacious, modern floor plans, luxury finishes, high ceilings and eco-friendly features. Residents will also have access to an on-site co-working space, clubhouse, two-story gym, dog park, rooftop lounge, spa pool and indoor/outdoor lounge area, game room, and easy access to Central Trail.

The project is led by investment firm Hunt Companies. Construction will be led by KWA Construction, while leasing and management of the property will be led by ZRS Management.

"As Richardson attracts more leading technology and innovation companies our population continues to grow, and we need partners like Hunt Companies to help us meet our housing demands," Mayor Paul Voelker said in the press release. "The Caroline Eastside will provide critical capacity in high-end multifamily living while creating an upscale resident experience in a vibrant area of Richardson."

Preleasing from the temporary office onsite will begin in quarter four 2023 with move-ins scheduled to begin in 2025. For more information, contact [here](http://heath.townsend@huntcompanies.com/).

title: Haggard Farm development going vertical in coming months
text:
Markdown Content:
Construction has begun on a Plano mixed-use development that is 170 years in the making.

The $750 million [Haggard Farm](https://stillwatercapital.com/properties/haggard-farms/) development held a groundbreaking ceremony Dec. 11, and will begin vertical construction in “the coming months,” Stillwater Capital Managing Director Clay Roby confirmed.

**At a glance**

The 142-acre plot at the southeast corner of Spring Creek Parkway and Parkwood Boulevard was one of many bought by the Haggard family in the early 1850s, and it’s one of the last remaining undeveloped.

Discussions to develop the land began in the mid-2010s, and plans were eventually approved in 2021. After ongoing construction on infrastructure finishes, work on the first building, an apartment complex, will begin soon.

The Haggard family’s 150-year-old house still stands on the property. The house and the barn will be incorporated into the development, according to a city news release.

“Plano has always been really thoughtful about the people that created the city of Plano,” Mayor John Muns said. “They’re going to design it with the Haggard family in mind.”

**Zooming out**

Only 4% of Plano’s land is undeveloped, and the 142-acres planned for Haggard Farm is one of the city’s largest chunks left, Plano Planning Director Christina Day said.

“When you have that much land area that’s developed, you have so many stakeholders,” she said. “Every piece of land that’s undeveloped has a lot of neighbors, people that have a strong interest in what happens there.”

Muns added that the city has to be “intentional” when planning to fill the remaining open space.

“Green field development is very limited these days,” Muns said. “I think it’s really important for us to really be thoughtful and intentional on what we do with what we have left.”

Day said that the city’s future land use designation for the Haggard Farm space has not changed for around two decades.

“The city’s had a fairly consistent vision for this for at least 20 years or so. ... That patience really pays off over time because you end up developing something that works well and is functional because you did not just respond to the trends of the moment,” she said. “Things change, and you have to update your plan, but at the same time, consistency really lends to the overall quality.”

**The specifics**

Construction of a new road connecting Spring Creek to Parkwood across the development was finished late last year, Plano Lead Planner Donna Sepulvado said.

The new road, called Pinehaven Drive, encompasses more than 350,000 square for its total right of way, and it paved the way for future development. Day confirmed that the road had to be finished to start construction.

The first of two 350-unit multifamily developments, located just west of the park and just north of Pinehaven, is the first building to begin construction at Haggard Farm.

Phase 1 will also feature 187 townhomes on the south end of the property. A [January zoning change](https://communityimpact.com/dallas-fort-worth/plano-north/government/2026/01/08/750m-haggard-farm-development-moves-forward-with-new-townhomes/) expanded the townhomes from 13 acres to 18.8 acres by removing the administrative office buildings in the original plan, according to city documents.

The last piece of Phase 1 will be a retail district, anchored by an 8,000-square-foot restaurant and bar called The Almanac 1856 and a 16,000-square-foot event barn called Haggard Hall.

Sepulvado said plans for the retail district have been conditionally approved, and the developer is currently finishing engineering plans.

“It’ll have more of a nostalgic feeling to it, at least in the retail part,” Muns said. “I think it will bring something really unique. ... As big as Plano is, I don’t think we have anything like that.”

**What’s next**

The first phase of construction—including the apartment building, retail district and townhomes—is expected to be finished in

title: Plano officials to consider senior living development at Park Boulevard, Preston Road
text:
Markdown Content:
A new senior independent living facility could be coming to west Plano, pending a rezoning request and public hearing.

At their Sept. 2 [meeting](https://planotx.new.swagit.com/videos/354223), Plano Planning and Zoning commissioners voted to call a public hearing for [items](https://content.civicplus.com/api/assets/f81a925e-c488-4646-a90a-58927bff7a6f) tied to a proposal to redevelop the former Plano Athletic Center site, which closed June 30, into a new Watermere senior living facility.

**What you need to know**

The proposed project would be a new Watermere independent living and active adult facility, similar to locations in Frisco and [McKinney](https://communityimpact.com/dallas-fort-worth/mckinney/real-estate/2025/08/14/senior-living-community-watermere-mckinney-opens-first-building-welcomes-residents/).

Trevor Armstrong, development manager for Integrated Real Estate Group, said the team has met with nearby business owners and homeowners associations since spring and held a community meeting in May, and they have not received any opposition to the changes.

Under Plano’s zoning ordinance, all property owners within a planned development district must consent to changes to the district.

With the public hearing now authorized, property owners within 200 feet of the zoning district and residential neighborhoods up to 500 feet away will be formally notified.

**Zooming in**

[Integrated Real Estate Group](https://www.integratedreg.com/), a Southlake-based company that builds and manages senior housing across Texas, is seeking to amend the planned development district that covers 108 acres at the southeast corner of Park Boulevard and Preston Road.

While not previously an allowed use, development changes brought on by Senate Bill 840 would allow the independent living facility in the space by right.

Assistant Director of Planning Michael Bell said the project still requires a zoning change, however, due to the proposed height of the development.

“It would be a zoning change either way under the current law or the new law,” Bell said.

**Looking ahead**

A public hearing date has not been set, and the developer plans to submit their formal zoning application Sept. 8, according to [city documents](https://content.civicplus.com/api/assets/f81a925e-c488-4646-a90a-58927bff7a6f).

## 2025 City of Plano Resident Survey Executive Summary 

Purpose 

ETC Institute administered a resident survey for the City of Plano in June and July of 2025. The survey was administered as part of the City’s ongoing effort to identify and respond to resident concerns. This was the sixth resident survey that ETC Institute administered for the City of Plano, with the first being in 2012. 

Methodology 

The seven-page survey, cover letter, and postage-paid return envelope was mailed to a random sample of households throughout the City of Plano. The cover letter explained the purpose of the survey and included a URL link for residents who preferred to complete the survey online. After the surveys were mailed, ETC Institute followed up with residents to encourage participation. The goal was to receive at least 400 completed surveys. This goal was met, with a total of 448 households completing a survey. The results for the random sample of 448 households have a 95% level of confidence with a precision of at least +/- 4.6%. In order to better understand how well services are being delivered by the City, ETC Institute geocoded the home address of respondents to the survey. The map below shows the physical distribution of survey respondents based on the locations of their homes. 2025 City of Plano Resident Survey: Findings Report ETC Institute (2025) Page iii 

## 2025 City of Plano Resident Survey Executive Summary 

This report contains the following: 

• a summary of the methodology for administering the survey and major findings 

• charts showing the overall results for the 2025 survey, along with comparisons to the results from the 2022 and 2019 surveys (Section 1) 

• benchmarking data that show how the results for the City of Plano compare to other cities in the United States and the state of Texas (Section 2) 

• Importance-Satisfaction analysis that identifies priorities for investment (Section 3) 

• tabular data showing the overall results for all questions on the survey (Section 4) 

• a copy of the cover letter and survey instrument (Section 5) 

Interpretation of “Don’t Know” Responses.  The percentage of persons who provide “don’t know” responses is important because it often reflects the level of utilization of city services. For graphing purposes, the percentage of “don’t know” responses has been excluded to facilitate valid comparisons with data from previous years. The percentage of “don’t know” responses for each question is provided in the Tabular Data section of this report. When the “don’t know” responses have been excluded, the text of this report will indicate that the responses have been excluded with the phrase “ who had an opinion .” 

Major Findings 

Overall Satisfaction with City Services 

 The major categories of city services with the highest levels of satisfaction, based upon the combined percentage of “very satisfied” and “satisfied” responses among residents who had an opinion were: fire services (95%), emergency medical services (93%), library services (92%), and 9-1-1 services related to police/fire/EMS (91%). 

 Based on the sum of their top four choices, the services that residents thought were the most important for the City to emphasize over the next two years were: (1) police services, (2) fire services, (3) emergency medical services, and (4) maintenance of City streets. 

Perceptions of the City 

 Most residents have a positive perception of the City of Plano. Ninety-one percent (91%) of residents, 

who had an opinion, are either “very satisfied” or “satisfied” with the overall quality of services provided by the City. Eighty-nine percent (89%) of residents, who had an opinion, are either “very satisfied” or “satisfied” with the overall quality of life in Plano. 2025 City of Plano Resident Survey: Findings Report ETC Institute (2025) Page iv 

## 2025 City of Plano Resident Survey Executive Summary 

Communication 

 Seventy-four percent (74%) of residents currently obtain information about Plano from the City’s website; 59% obtain information about the City from the City’s social media pages, and 43% obtain information from direct mail pieces. 

 The City communication services with the highest levels of satisfaction, based upon the combined percentage of “very satisfied” and “satisfied” responses among residents who had an opinion were: usefulness of the information available on the City’s website (73%) and availability of information about government operations (61%). 

Perceptions of Safety in Plano 

 Most of the residents surveyed (98%), who had an opinion, felt “very safe” or “safe” in their neighborhood during the day; 93% of the residents surveyed, who had an opinion , felt “very safe” or “safe” overall in Plano. 

Sustainability and Environmental Services 

 Forty-five percent (45%) of residents indicated the issue they are most concerned with as it affects their daily life is litter in the community and local waterways. Other issues of concern include: water quality (creeks/streams) (42%), local air quality (40%), and mobility and transportation (40%). 

 Sixty-five percent (65%) of the residents surveyed, who had an opinion, were “very satisfied” or “satisfied” with the access and availability of information about sustainability initiatives and programs, and 65% were satisfied with opportunities for community engagement through Live Green in Plano programs. 

Public Library System 

 Based on the sum of their top five choices, the areas that residents feel should be the top priorities for Plano libraries are: 1) helpful, friendly staff, 2) access to eMaterials, 3) physical materials for checkout, 4) in-person and virtual/online educational programs and classes, and 5) free WiFi, computers and internet access. 

 Based on the sum of their top five choices, the library outreach programming options that residents feel are most important for the community are: 1) Art and Culture, 2) STEAM, 3) Early Learning, 4) Workforce Development, and 5) Business and Entrepreneurship. 2025 City of Plano Resident Survey: Findings Report ETC Institute (2025) Page v 

## 2025 City of Plano Resident Survey Executive Summary 

Parks and Recreation 

 Ninety-three percent (93%) of residents feel the City is “exceeding” or “meeting” their expectations in the appearance of public building landscapes; 91% feel the City is “exceeding” or “meeting” their expectations in the cleanliness of recreation facilities, and 90% feel the City is “exceeding” or “meeting” their expectations in the cleanliness of City parks. 

 Based on the sum of their top five choices, the areas that residents feel should be the top priorities for Plano parks and recreation over the next ten years are: 1) trail connections, 2) additional land for parks, 3) renovating playgrounds, 4) adult recreation center, and 5) art centers/studios. 

Public Works/Engineering 

 The public works/engineering services with the highest levels of satisfaction, based upon the combined percentage of “very satisfied” and “satisfied” responses among residents who had an opinion , were: the traffic signal system (48%), pedestrian safety (45%), and bicycle safety (32%). 

Property Standards 

 The statements pertaining to property standards that had the highest levels of agreement, based upon the combined percentage of “strongly agree” and “agree” responses among residents who had an opinion , were: “property standards are necessary to maintain or improve my neighborhood” (79%), “the item I reported was corrected or staff explained why it was not a violation” (56%), and “staff provide courteous and timely service (55%). 

 Fifty-eight percent (58%) of residents feel the appearance of their neighborhood has stayed the same over the past three years; 15% feel it has improved, 23% feel it has gotten worse, and 5% did not have an opinion. 2025 City of Plano Resident Survey: Findings Report ETC Institute (2025) Page vi

## 2025 City of Plano Resident Survey Executive Summary 

Investment Priorities 

Recommended Priorities. In order to help the City identify investment priorities for the future, ETC Institute conducted an Importance-Satisfaction (I-S) analysis. This analysis examined the importance that residents placed on each City service and the level of satisfaction with each service. 

By identifying services of high importance and low satisfaction, the analysis identified which services will have the most impact on overall satisfaction with City services. If the City wants to improve its overall satisfaction rating, the City should prioritize investments in services with the highest Importance Satisfaction (I-S) ratings. Details regarding the methodology for the analysis are provided in Section 3 of this report. # 2 Benchmarking Analysis 2025 City of Plano Resident Survey: Findings Report ETC Institute (2025) Page 50 Benchmarking Analysis 

Overview 

ETC Institute’s DirectionFinder® program was originally developed in 1999 to help community leaders use statistically valid community survey data as a tool for making better decisions. Since November 1999, the survey has been administered in more than 300 cities and counties in 43 states. Most participating communities conduct the survey on an annual or biennial basis. 

This report contains benchmarking data from two sources: (1) a national survey that was administered by ETC Institute during the summer of 2023 to a random sample of over 10,000 residents in the continental United States and (2) a regional survey that was administered by ETC Institute during the summer of 2023 to a random sample of residents living in the state of Texas.

# 3 Importance-Satisfaction Analysis 2025 City of Plano Resident Survey: Findings Report ETC Institute (2025) Page 58 Importance-Satisfaction Analysis 

Overview 

Today, community leaders have limited resources which need to be targeted to activities that are of the most benefit to their citizens. Two of the most important criteria for decision making are (1) to target resources toward services of the highest importance to citizens; and (2) to target resources toward those 

services where citizens are the least satisfied. 

The Importance ‐Satisfaction (I ‐S) rating is a unique tool that allows public officials to better understand both of these highly important decision ‐making criteria for each of the services they are providing. The Importance ‐Satisfaction (I ‐S) rating is based on the concept that public agencies will maximize overall customer satisfaction by emphasizing improvements in those areas where the level of satisfaction is relatively low, and the perceived importance of the service is relatively high. 

The rating is calculated by summing the percentage of responses for items selected as the first, second, third, and fourth most important services for the City to provide. The sum is then multiplied by 1 minus the percentage of respondents who indicated they were positively satisfied with the City’s performance in the related area (the sum of the ratings of 4 and 5 on a 5 ‐point scale excluding “Don’t Know” responses). “Don’t Know” responses are excluded from the calculation to ensure the satisfaction ratings among service categories are comparable. 

I-S Rating = Importance x (1 -Satisfaction) 

Example of the Calculation 

Respondents were asked to identify the major City services that are most important for the City to provide. Nearly forty ‐five percent (44.7%) of households selected “maintenance of City streets” as one of the most important services for the City to provide. 

With regard to satisfaction, 40% of respondents surveyed rated “maintenance of City streets” as a “4” or “5” on a 5 ‐point scale (where “5” means “Very Satisfied”) excluding “Don’t Know” responses. The I ‐Srating was calculated by multiplying the sum of the most important percentages by one minus the sum of the satisfaction percentages. In this example, 44.7% was multiplied by 60% ( 1‐ 0.40). This calculation yielded an I ‐S rating of 0.2682, which ranked first out of twenty ‐one categories of major City services analyzed. 2025 City of Plano Resident Survey: Findings Report ETC Institute (2025) Page 59 Importance-Satisfaction Analysis 

The maximum rating is 1.00 and would be achieved when 100% of the respondents select an item as one of their top four choices of importance and 0% indicate they are positively satisfied with the delivery of the service. 

The lowest rating is 0.00 and could be achieved under either of the following two situations: 

• If 100% of the respondents were positively satisfied with the delivery of the service 

• If none (0%) of the respondents selected the service as one of the four most important areas. 

Interpreting the Ratings 

Ratings that are greater than or equal to 0.20 identify areas that should receive significantly more emphasis. Ratings from 0.10 to 0.20 identify service areas that should receive increased emphasis. Ratings less than 0.10 should continue to receive the current level of emphasis. 

• Definitely Increase Emphasis (I ‐S > 0.20) 

• Increase Current Emphasis (I ‐S = 0.10  ‐ 0.20) 

• Maintain Current Emphasis (I ‐S < 0.10)

# Importance-Satisfaction Analysis 

Importance-Satisfaction Matrix Analysis 

The Importance-Satisfaction rating is based on the concept that public agencies will maximize overall customer satisfaction by emphasizing improvements in those areas where the level of satisfaction is relatively low, and the perceived importance of the service is relatively high. ETC Institute developed an Importance-Satisfaction Matrix to display the perceived importance of major services that were assessed on the survey against the perceived quality of service delivery. The two axes on the matrix represent Satisfaction (vertical) and relative Importance (horizontal). 

The I-S (Importance-Satisfaction) matrix should be interpreted as follows. 

 Continued Emphasis (above average importance and above average satisfaction). This area shows where the City is meeting customer expectations. Items in this area have a significant impact on the customer’s overall level of satisfaction. The City should maintain (or slightly increase) emphasis on items in this area. 

 Exceeding Expectations (below average importance and above average satisfaction). This area shows where the City is performing significantly better than customers expect the City to perform. Items in this area do not significantly affect the overall level of satisfaction that residents have with City services. The City should maintain (or slightly decrease) emphasis on items in this area. 

 Opportunities for Improvement (above average importance and below average satisfaction). 

This area shows where the City is not performing as well as residents expect the City to perform. This area has a significant impact on customer satisfaction, and the City should DEFINITELY increase emphasis on items in this area. 

 Less Important (below average importance and below average satisfaction). This area shows where the City is not performing well relative to its performance in other areas; however, this area is generally considered to be less important to residents. This area does not significantly affect overall satisfaction with City services because the items are less important to residents. The agency should maintain current levels of emphasis on items in this area.

# QUESTION 5 1 CONT. 

# Which of the following do you think would be beneficial? 

Question 5: Which of the following do you think would be beneficial? 

Respondents were asked to select all that apply. Percentage Responses 

Registration and licensing of STRs 68% 4,178 Limiting density of STRs (limit number of STRs in a certain area) 55% 3,329 Require public health and safety inspections of STRs 51% 3,091 Designating an emergency contact for STRs 48% 2,920 Restrict STRs to certain areas of town 47% 2,877 Study or review the effect of STRs on the cost of housing for permanent residents 41% 2,516 Require STR owners to complete specialized training 41% 2,492 Study or review the effect of STRs on the availability of housing for permanent residents 39% 2,388 Restrict STRs to neighborhoods with mandatory Homeowners Associations, which could regulate STRs at the neighborhood level 38% 2,339 Restrict STRs to certain types of housing (i.e. only on certain lot sizes) 32% 1,942 Allow neighborhoods to opt-in to allowing STRs 32% 1,930 No regulations are needed / appropriate for STRs 6% 342 Other 11% 653 

Totals 508% 30,997 

Number of Respondents to Question 5: 6,102 

# Note: Of those that answered "other," 434 chose to write in a short answer response. Those responses, and the short answer responses in subsequent questions, are in the appendix at the end of this report. 

CITY OF PLANO STR STUDY I COMMUNITY SURVEY RESULTS 13 QUESTION 8 1 CONT. 

# Have you personally experienced or witnessed any of the following benefits associated with short-term rentals in Plano? 

Question 8: Have you personally experienced or witnessed any of the following benefits associated with short-term rentals in Plano? 

Respondents were asked to select all that apply. Percentage Responses 

None 78% 4,765 

Availability of convenient lodging for visitors & guests 14% 849 

Availability of temporary housing for remote, seasonal, or traveling professionals 14% 830 

Availability of unique lodging experience for visitors & guests 10% 610 

Benefit to local economy by increased business patronage 8% 464 

Income derived in full or in part from STRs 7% 415 

Increased tourism 6% 378 

Exceptional hospitality 5% 323 

Improvement to property conditions 5% 323 

Local job creation 4% 262 

Improved lifestyle / livelihood for local homeowners 3% 207 

Availability of new event spaces and venues 3% 152 

Other 2% 140 

Totals 159% 9,718 

Number of Respondents to Question 8: 6,105 

CITY OF PLANO STR STUDY I COMMUNITY SURVEY RESULTS 17 

# Note : Of those that answered "other," 434 chose to write in a short answer response. Those responses, and the short answer responses in a subsequent questions, are in the appendix at the end of this report. Plano STR Study Survey Short Answers Question 5 (436 Responses) 1

Which of the following do you think would be beneficial? 

1. Change law to forbid future STR in zoned residential (grandfathering existing ones if registered by some deadline). 2. Have repeat offenders lose registration. 1. Sunset period for current STR Owner Operator to close their business within 6 months 2. Require Realtors to disclose where STR’s are located. 3. Require City officials to disclose real estate holdings and relationships 4. Establish a permanent CAP on total number of short term rentals in the city 5. Require a minimum physical distance from schools. 6. Provide a mechanism for permanent removal of an STR after two violations of regulation, and or one egregious violation. 7. Create criminal penalties for operators, who intentionally attempt to circumvent the law. 2 violations loose your right to STR Ability to revoke STR permit for that house, after so many violations or police reports According to current zoning Plano laws they shouldn’t be allowed. Do not allow them! Enforce your laws! Additional Fines for Owner if Violation occurs Additional police in areas with STR’s. City task force to review sober living homes. Additional taxes should be imposed on STRs - a negative Homestead Exception if you will. STRs would be taxed at a higher rate and be ineligible for a Homestead Exception. AirBNB's (Short-Term-Rentals) should NOT be allowed in residential zoned neighborhoods! AirBNB's (Short-Term-Rentals) should NOT be allowed in zoned residential neighborhoods! All of these options sound like red tape. It would be significantly more straightforward to just ban them across the board. Allow citizens to vote for or against STRs Allow neighborhoods to OPT OUT of allowing STRs. A limit on maximum guests allowed, regardless of property size, might be appropriate. The areas experiencing problems seem to have larger homes and are thus more prone to big groups and/or parties. Allow neighborhoods to opt OUT of STRs Allow neighbors to "red flag" a STR and remove it after police are called to the home Allow No Short Term Rentals Period!! Short Term Rentals are a revenue making entity. Which means they fall into the commercial zoning same as hotels, motels, and store front shops/strip mall centers. Not even in the multi-family category. Plano City Council needs to stop all STR with no more allow/permitted. They Do Not Increase Anything, Any part of Plano's Property Values. Only decrease property value. Allow STRs only in non residential areas. An escalating monetary fine for public nuisance or citations with a rental. STR rental ban when renters use the property for criminal purposes. Hold property owners accountable for commercial liability insurance. An STR was behind my house and it was horrible and I was often very scared . No more please. Assuming registration and licensing is required for STR. The license info and complain phone number should be posted at designated location on property for neighbors to report problems and complains. Background checks for short term renters to ensure safety of my children background checks on all renters Ban Ban Ban all Ban all short term rentals Ban all STR in Plano. Plano is not a vacation destination. It’s residential. We don’t need transient people who don’t care about our city . Ban all within city. Ban short term rentals in residential zoned areas Ban STR in residential zoned areas. They are a business and thus should be in business zoned areas Ban STR, maintain the Plano that families have enjoyed and expect. Ban STR's, there are enough Motels around the city Ban STRs Ban STRs Ban STRs Ban STRs Plano STR Study Survey Short Answers Question 5 (436 Responses) 2

Which of the following do you think would be beneficial? 

Ban STRs Ban STRs city wide. Do not study and drag a decision out for a year. The negative effect on my neighborhood is here NOW. Do not attempt to delegate the regulations and decisions to HOAs as this survey suggest in the way it is written. City council should do its job and ban all strs. Ban STRs completely. They would devalue our home living experience. Ban STRs from all residential neighborhoods. STRs are commercial businesses. Enforce zoning to stop STR commercial businesses from operating in residential neighborhoods. Ban STRs from residential neighborhoods. STRs are commercial businesses. Neighborhoods are not zoned commercial. Enforce the zoning rules to prevent STRs from operating in residential neighborhoods. Ban STRs in all Single Family Zoned Neighborhoods Ban STRs in plano. Give the city back to people who actually live here Ban STRs in residential neighborhoods. Ban STRs in the city of Plano Ban STRs totally in neighborhoods Ban STRs within the City of Plano BAN THEM Ban them ban them Ban them BAN THEM ALTOGETHER Ban them altogether. Not having an HOA should not be a punishment BAN THEM COMPLETELY. HAVE ONE NEARBY MY 20-YEAR RES. WITH MACHINE GUN FIRED. NOT FUNNY. Ban them entirely. Single family homes are zoned residential NOT commercial. No exceptions. Any council person supporting STRs is not bettering the community and must be replaced. Ban them from Plano Ban them outright in neighborhoods Ban them. Other cities in Texas have banned them. We don't want them here! Ban use of single family homes as multi individual rentals. For example renting out multiple rooms in home to multiple individuals City of Plano should establish a monitoring department to specifically track issues with STRs and publicize issues on a quarterly basis and available to the public. Residents in a neighborhood should be notified when an STR has been registered in their neighborhood (including address of property). Classify as a hotel so that STRs would have to meet all the requirements as a hotel Collect hotel taxes from Airbnb similar to Farmers Branch and The Colony to add to COP. And do study to find out how much revenue and jobs STR add to the economy of COP. Collect hotel taxes from STR to add to COP coffers. So study to find out revenue impact of STR on COP economy. Commercial Zoned Areas Only Complete BAN Complete ban Complete ban of Short Term Rentals Completely ban Completely ban STR within Plano Conduct study on the effect on housing values. Consider impact on the quality of neighborhood LIFE rather than impact on Prop values. I have lived in a neighborhood almost 40 years and see the negative impacts of short term rentals Consider minimum night stays to 2+nights to keep parties down Consider STRs as the businesses that they are and zone them out of residential neighborhoods. Create strict regulations regarding lawn/property maintenance for STRs Plano STR Study Survey Short Answers Question 5 (436 Responses) 3

Which of the following do you think would be beneficial? 

Crime Watch Decrease the number of STRs period. It is causing problems for long term renters!!! Deposit money with the City for prompt cleanup and maintenance if homeowner fails to be responsible for these items. Develop Event Regulations - no more than x number of people to any property. Disallow STRs completely within the city limits. Disallow them completely Do NOT allow any STR in any residential neighborhoods Do not allow Do not allow in neighborhoods DO NOT ALLOW Short term rentals at all Do not allow SRTs do not allow str Do not allow STR at all. Many cities do this in the US, why not here? Do NOT allow STR in Plano. It brings no good to our family friendly neighborhoods!! Do NOT allow STR in Plano. Leave that problem to cities who don’t know how to govern (San Fran, Austin…liberal towns) Do not allow STR in Plano. The neighborhoods were zoned for Single-Family dwelling, and many have small children…these are not designated as business rentals…that is what hotels are for! Do not allow STR in residential neighborhoods - only commercially zones Do not allow STR in residential single family area Do not allow STR. Require rentals to be a minimum of 6 months. Do not allow STR. If I wanted to live by a hotel I would have bought next to one Do not allow STRs Do not allow STRs Do not allow STRs Do not allow STRs Do not allow STRs .... period Do not allow STRs (less than 6 months) in any Plano property Do not allow STRs at the City level. Do not push to the HOAs to manage. Do not allow STRs in residential areas Do NOT allow STRs to operate in any residentially zoned single family neighborhood. Do not allow STRs within City of Plano Do not allow them at all Do not allow them at all! Do not allow them in Plano. Do not allow them in Plano. There are negative stories online DO NOT ALLOW THEM! Do not allow them. I already had to call the police for shooting on Peachtree lane where the you g man from Allen high school was shot. No STR’s. Period. Do not allow them. They are ruining my neighborhood. We have had multiple issues on my street with these. Do not waste my Tax dollars on any STRs, none this no need for all this. Don't allow any more STRs in residential neighborhoods. don't allow in single family neighborhoods, HOMES NOT HOTELS The one near me ended up as a brotel DO not want short term rentals anywhere single family; total ban on short term IF the owners and their renters acted responsibly there would be a conversation going on about short term rentals I have been impacted by both the brotel and then the one were the shootings occurred Don't allow them at all! Don't allow them here. Crime will go up Plano STR Study Survey Short Answers Question 5 (436 Responses) 4

Which of the following do you think would be beneficial? 

Don't allow them. Don't allow whole house rentals. Renting a room while the owner lives there is normally ok. Don’t allow in single family neighborhoods Don’t allow STR at all Don’t allow STR in neighborhoods Don’t allow stR in Plano Don’t allow STRs Don’t allow STRs in areas of single family housing Don’t allow them Don’t allow them Don’t allow them Don’t allow them all Don’t allow them at all. Don’t allow them at all. Don’t allow them at all. Don’t allow them in any residential neighborhood Don’t allow them in residential neighborhoods - period or within a proximity to schools where children are. Too many predators. Don’t allow them in residential neighborhoods. Either none allowed or follow Arlington rules Eliminate all STR in single family homes Eliminate in single family neighborhoods Eliminate STR's; they are business in residential zones. We purchased our homes based on zoned single family residence. Eliminate str’s altogether. Full stop. Eliminate STRs from Plano city limits Eliminate them completely encourage something to be done at the State level, rather than spin wheels locally. If this state can try to ban abortions, they should have no trouble trying to ban anything else under the sun. enforce residential zoning regulations. short term rentals are not residential, and should be treated as such. Ensure laws don't hinder owners from dealing with tenants who are not complying with rental agrements. Ensure neighborhood STRs are taxed at double the rate of other commercial motels and move to ban them entirely. Even voluntary home owners alliances shall have the power to regulate STRs. In addition, the property must be registered as an STR and property owner should not be granted homestead exemption on that property Extra Income or Property taxes Fines if any issues. Take away ability if any issues are reported. City needs to know which websites property is being advertised on. Copy of ad Fire code inspection / increased liability insurance. Owner must treat the property as the business it has become. Follow existing zoning single family zoned areas - STRs are hotels and therefore illegal Follow the existing zoning laws and prohibit STRs completely from neighborhoods of single-family homes. Follow zoning laws. Treat like hotels. Can't build a hotel in middle of neighborhood. For the safety and comfort of the vast majority of homeowners within Plano, make STRs illegal. The upside is minimal but the potential downside could be tragic. For the most part STRs shouldn't be treated any differently than rental property. Have a minimum stay of 30 days in STR Have progressive fine enforcement for multiple complaints. Having a published contact for STRs. The owner should be accessible to neighbors and if there is no homeowners org, they should have maintenance rules Plano STR Study Survey Short Answers Question 5 (436 Responses) 5

Which of the following do you think would be beneficial? 

Heavily taxed. Must register STR with City. City should charge $1,500 minimum annual fee. Otherwise let neighborhoods with HOAs decide for their own community Higher property taxes for STRs vs LTRs and Homesteads. Hire more police and city staff to help with issues that may arise as a result of STR’s.. Homeowner Associations are not built in baby-sitters. STR should not be in any residential area. Hotel tax already applies, why is the city turning down revenue?! I am totally against STRs in Plano neighborhoods I do not believe short term rentals are beneficial in residential neighborhoods. The should be banned and removed as they are not compatible with permanent community. They create more problems, crimes, and cause many safety and security issues in the neighborhood. I do not favor any neighborhood STR. Adversely affects our HOMES where we live and are already affected by traffic noise (very loud cars and pick-ups) I DO NOT WANT A HOTEL 2 HOUSES FROM MINE - PERIOD !!!!!!!!!!! This is a NEIGHBORHOOD NOT A HOTELHOOD... YOU BETTER BAN STR in PLANO !! I do not want a short term rental in my neighborhood. Too much risk in my opinion. I bought a house to live in as a home (and paid my hard earned money!) and consider my neighborhood a home as well. I do not want short-term rentals in Plano, TX. No benefits. Brings crime and trouble. I don't think that STR's belong in any single family residential neighborhood because they cause a severe negative impact on our neighborhoods. If Plano wants to consider allowing STR's in a very small designated area like Arlington did, they will need to be regulated very closely. The reality is that if there is a need for daily, weekend, weekly rentals, hotel developers will fill the need by developing more properties. Leave the SF homes for homeowners and long term rentals. We have a shortage! I don't want short-term rentals in my neighborhood I don't want STR in my neighborhood. I believe it's too difficult to regulate. I don’t think anywhere in Plano neighborhoods should there be STR’s. It will devalue our properties and STR’s are difficult to manage. I don’t want any short term rentals. We live here. We have a vested interest in the community and don’t need people coming in and disrupting our peace I really don't want STRs around my home at all. I STRs in residential neighborhoods with single family homes. Only allow STRs in high density house if areas (I.e. apartments, condos, and townhomes). I think HOAs can govern their own neighborhoods. But neighborhoods without HOAs should be able to what they want with their property. Hopefully landlords are respectful in renting out their properties with some rental rules in place. I think they should be banned. We have hotels and resorts. I truly like the training suggestion. I believe these should be updated and renewed. Also, if house is close to other homes, there should be a minimum times per month they are allowed to be rented out without owner living on the property and keeping situation under control. We only go to STR that are in quiet area with plenty of open land. We go to be quiet, not have a party! We leave the property clean, kept up and show with great respect how we appreciate the time there. I would like to better understand how other similar cities have done this and their results. Ideally, I would like to see STR totally prohibited. Ideally, I would prefer that shortterm rentals are prohibited in all neighborhoods. If owners are registered and licensed, then also have consequences for repeat offenders such as revoking the STR permit, while imposing fines for operating without permit/license. If you require a permit for garage sale, why not STR? KEY ISSUES 

In preparing Module 1B, particular care has been taken to address important factors that apply to all defined terms and standards in the UDC but are particularly important when considering residential land uses. These include: 

• Defensibility: Definitions should have consistent language. Nuances should be respected while 

making efforts to simplify standards. Language should be logical and consistent. AGENDA ITEM NO. 3 (04/24/25) PAGE 3 OF 10 

• Enforceability: Definitions that rely on the relationships between people, whether immediate 

family, roommates, or landlord and lessee, are difficult to enforce. Definitions and the standards that flow from them should use metrics that are easy to observe. 

• Health & Safety: Zoning standards are grounded in health and safety considerations, to provide 

a suitable living environment through compatible and orderly development. Affordability concerns put pressure on the market to provide alternatives to traditional living arrangements. Some considerations include: 

o Does a resident have full or partial authority to keep his or her living quarters safe? 

o What is the level of security for a resident? 

o How much access does a resident, and other individuals, have to the property? 

o How intensive are the living arrangements? 

o How much privacy is enjoyed? 

• Clarity: Terms should be defined as needed, and the need for director interpretations should be 

minimized. New housing forms have evolved, resulting in additional considerations. Things that are alike should be treated the same. Things that are substantially different should be acknowledged. 

• Community Perception & Expectations: The proposed changes make efforts to balance 

competing concerns of the community, such as preservation of existing neighborhoods, property values, property rights, housing accessibility, and housing affordability. The community is especially sensitive to land use regulations that affect their neighborhood and takes pride in the quality of life that Plano provides. Changes to residential land uses and definitions should be sensitive to community expectations while recognizing individual property rights. 

For example, the “Single-Family Dwelling” use as currently defined allows for the building to be occupied by not more than one household, and a household might be many variations, including a family, a group of adult roommates, a single-person household operating a home occupation, or a caregiver and their patients. Although each of these can be legal uses of the property, only one of these groups is captured in the defined term, which can create friction if community expectations do not match the way the property is used. 

SUBSTANTIAL CHANGES 

The proposed changes are a shift in how residential and institutional dwelling uses are organized and defined, and, in turn, how they will function when development standards are considered in Module 4. 

These changes are explained further in this section, and a comparison between the current and proposed definitions is provided in Attachment B. AGENDA ITEM NO. 3 (04/24/25) PAGE 4 OF 10 

Separating Form (Building and Site Layout) and Function (Land Use) 

As discussed above, it is important to thoughtfully evaluate the intent, function, and outcomes of the residential land use definitions. The current land use definitions sometimes combine building form and function. For example, the “Single-Family Residence Attached (SF-A)” zoning district controls building form, and the “Single-Family Residence (Attached)” use definition includes information on how the building is constructed: 

Single-Family Residence (Attached): A dwelling that is part of a structure containing 3 or more dwellings, each designed and constructed for occupancy by one family, with each dwelling attached by a common wall to another with a minimum length of attachment of 20 feet, in which each dwelling is located on a separate platted lot (unless the dwelling is part of a planned residential development approved without separate platted lots); except that 20% of the total dwellings in a single family attached project may be included in structures containing only 2 dwellings. 

A new framework for residential uses is proposed to isolate form and function, to provide a clearer distinction between the use of a property and the site design on a property. Form is detailed in zoning districts (Module 1A) and design standards (Module 4) while functions are described in the definitions in this module. 

New and revised land use definitions describe the activity that occurs inside the building (function). This is intended to clarify that a variety of uses continue to be permitted in any one residential building form; for example, a single detached residence building could contain a “Private Residence,” “Shared Residence,” or “Community Care Home” use . These uses are explained in more detail in the next section. 

Current vs. Proposed Definitions Framework 

The current Zoning Ordinance uses a framework of defined terms and land uses to regulate housing, which can be summarized as follows: 

• Household and Dwelling Unit form the foundation of all residential definitions, based on the function, number of people, and their relationships. 

o Household : A domestic unit that resides in and shares in common a single dwelling unit and consists of one or more individuals related by blood, marriage, adoption or recognized legal union or guardianship, and not more than 4 adult unrelated individuals, plus any minor children, or persons residing in a household care facility .

o Dwelling Unit : A building or portion of a building which is arranged, occupied, or intended to be occupied as living quarters of a family and including facilities for food preparation, sleeping, and sanitation. 

• Dwelling (Multifamily) , Dwelling (Single-family) , and Dwelling (Two-family) describe three types of buildings and the number of Dwelling Units or Households each building may or must contain. AGENDA ITEM NO. 3 (04/24/25) PAGE 5 OF 10 

• Twenty-three defined residential and institutional dwelling land uses, such as Single-Family Residence (Attached) , Single-Family Residence (Detached) , and Multifamily Residence ,build on, and may (or may not) refer back to the dwelling definitions above. Some definitions do not specify a dwelling type. 

The various dwelling and land use definitions do not consistently refer to families or households, which can create confusion and misplaced community expectations. For example, the definition of the “Single-Family Residence (Attached)” use provided above states occupation by one family, but the definition of “Dwelling (Single-family)” states occupation by one household: 

Dwelling (Single-family) : A building having accommodations for and occupied by not more than one household. 

According to  2023 Census data , one-third of households in Plano are non-family households. 

The proposed residential definitions are based on a new framework, with two foundational elements, described below, focusing on function, privacy, access, and number of rooms: 

• Dwelling (or Dwelling Unit) : A complete living space, further defined as a space that provides for the activities required for daily living which must include indoor areas for sleeping, bathing, and a Residential Kitchen. A Dwelling also includes the private outdoor leisure areas that form part of the living space. 

This is an update to the definition of “Dwelling Unit” that removes reference to occupation by a family. The three separately defined “Dwelling”-based form definitions are deleted. 

• Private Room : A living space within a Dwelling where adult occupants have individual control and enjoy a right to privacy and where other occupants in the same Dwelling can be legally excluded. A Private Room may be a suite including separate rooms for sleeping and bathing, but may not include a Residential Kitchen. 

A new definition of “Private Room” to describe an area of a residence where the occupant has total control over the space. Private rooms form the basis for separating the Private Residence, Shared Residence, Group Residence, and Residential Facility residence types further described below. Private rooms are areas that could be made available for separate rentals. 

The following residence and facility types were constructed using the two foundational elements above. Additional land uses also refer to these types (the chart on the next page lists land uses that would fall under each residence or facility type): 

• Private Residence : A Dwelling in which all adult occupants have access to the entire space with no legal right to exclusion from any portion of the property. 

This is a new land use definition to describe a household unit living together in any residential building typology. A “Private Residence” has no private rooms, as the whole dwelling is shared among the occupants. This is similar to the Housekeeping Unit definition in the current Zoning Ordinance; however, the Housekeeping Unit definition is not used in the Ordinance. 

Housekeeping Unit: A dwelling unit organized as a single entity in which members share common kitchen facilities and have access to all parts of the dwelling. AGENDA ITEM NO. 3 (04/24/25) PAGE 6 OF 10 

• Shared Residence : A Dwelling that includes not more than four Private Rooms, together with a Residential Kitchen that serves all occupants of the Dwelling. All occupants must have either private or shared access to areas for sleeping and bathing. 

This is a new land use definition to describe roommates with separate leases living together in any residential building typology. A “Shared Residence” may have up to four private rooms and is intended to align with the current definition of a “Household,” which allows up to four unrelated adults. 

• Group Residence : A Dwelling that includes at least five and not more than eight Private Rooms together with a Residential Kitchen that serves all occupants of the Dwelling. All occupants must have either private or shared access to areas for sleeping and bathing. 

This is a new definition for residence types with up to eight private rooms and is intended to align with the current definitions of a “Household Care Facility” and “Rehabilitation Care Facility,” which allow up to eight unrelated adults plus two caretakers. Three revised care home uses refer to this Group Residence definition and allow an additional two private rooms for the caretakers of the dwelling, but the updated Boarding House use only allows up to eight private rooms. 

• Residential Facility : A building or complex of buildings that includes at least nine Private Rooms designed and occupied as the living place of persons and where supervision is provided in the form of on-site staff or caretakers who may or may not also live on the premises. AResidential Facility also includes the private outdoor leisure areas that contribute to daily living. 

This is a new definition to help describe various institutional dwelling land uses. These would have nine or more private rooms available to the supervised occupants, to mark a clear distinction from the “Group Residence” land uses.

Institutional Dwellings 

Institutional dwelling refers to specialized facilities that provide housing in a supervised or caregiver setting. The existing land uses provide for the residence, care, and supervision of distinct groups of people; however, the definitions sometimes overlap, resulting in conflicting land use permissions. In the existing Ordinance, a “Household Care Institution” is not permitted in the same districts as an “Assisted Living Facility,” despite both allowing for the residence and care of the elderly or disabled. This may be due to the former also providing residence and care for persons temporarily displaced by fire, natural disaster, or financial setback, and for children who are neglected, abandoned, or orphaned. The proposed changes address each group individually, as summarized in the following chart.

Age restricted housing, defined as an “Independent Living Facility” in the current Ordinance and “Independent Living Residence” in the proposed UDC, will continue to be regulated the same as housing that is not age restricted, consistent with the comprehensive plan, a change that was made in 2023. “Independent Living Residence” is a sub-type of “Private Residence” or “Shared Residence,” with the only distinction being the age restriction. The draft use chart has been updated to match the permissions of “Independent Living Residence” to “Private Residence” and “Shared Residence.”

OTHER NOTABLE TOPICS 

While the majority of the changes in Module 1B are covered above, there are some additional changes that should be pointed out due to the impact they have on administration and organization of the code. These include: 

A. Backyard Cottages and Accessory Dwelling Units: Backyard cottages are currently regulated 

as a distinct land use in most single-family districts, whereas the Estate Development (ED) zoning district has specific regulations for accessory dwelling units. As part of the separation of building form and land use, “backyard cottage” has been removed from the use chart, and would instead be a Private or Shared Residence land use, subject to standards for accessory dwelling units, reviewed in Module 4. 

B. Hotel/Motel Definition: The current definition of hotels and motels includes a minimum of four 

rooms. The proposed UDC would have a different definition with a minimum of five rooms to clearly distinguish the use from a Shared Residence, which, where permitted, could be used as a Short-term Rental Residence. 

C. Housing Shelters: The current Ordinance has a use and definition for a Temporary Accessory 

Housing Shelter, but a permanent Housing Shelter is not a listed use. A new land use and definition are proposed in the UDC. 

D. Campground: Changes to state law in a recent legislative session brought forward discussion 

about where camping might be allowed. Adding this definition will help clarify the use allowances in the city. 

E. Dormitory: Facilities that offer long-term housing without supervision or care currently fall under 

the Boarding House (Single-Room Occupancy) land use definition. With the changes proposed in the revised Boarding House definition, new Dormitory definitions are proposed to accommodate Residential Facilities with more than eight Private Rooms. One definition applies to religious and educational dormitories, and the second applies to all other dormitories. 

F. Bunkhouse: This definition provides explicitly for a housing type in the market, similar to a hostel 

or group living quarters. This definition both provides opportunities for congregate living in a group setting and places a limit on congregate living in other housing types. For example, a Boarding House (a Group Residence, which is a Dwelling that includes at least five and not more than eight Private Rooms, providing housing to persons sharing living areas in common…) would be considered a Bunkhouse if providing more than nine beds for individual rental. SPECIFIC QUESTIONS 

While feedback on any aspect of Module 1B is welcome, the Committee is asked to consider the following specific questions when reviewing the first draft. When considering these questions, note that use-specific regulations, when needed, will be included in Module 4. 

1. Do the proposed foundational terms provide an improved framework for residential uses? 

The proposed UDC includes definitions for “Dwelling,” “Private Room,” “Private Residence,” “Shared Residence,” “Group Residence,” and “Residential Facility” to create a foundation for all of the defined residential and institutional dwelling land uses. The intent is to acknowledge and accommodate the variety of ways that housing is used while protecting the form and character of established neighborhoods. 

The Committee is asked to consider how this shift in defined land uses does (or does not) achieve the intended goals.

STAFF REPORT – PROCESS 

Module 1B (Residential, Institutional Dwelling, and Related Land Uses) has been posted to an online commenting platform to facilitate review and feedback. A version open to the public for commenting is available on  Konveio , and a password-protected version exclusively for the Committee is available on 

a separate webpage. The documents include a two-page “primer” for the public, intended to introduce the project and provide a very high-level summary of the proposed framework (Attachment C). 

Commenting on both the public and Committee documents will be closed on May 1, 2025. The public comments for both Modules 1A and 1B will be included in the May 15, 2025, meeting packet. 

Public comments will also be provided to the Commission and Council when Module 1 is presented at their meetings. All comments from the public and the Committee are part of the public record. 

HOW TO USE KONVEIO 

Both the public and Committee members are required to create an account when commenting on the documents. Committee members have received a link and password information to gain access to the Committee document in email communication. 

Comments can be posted anywhere on the document, and the commenter is able to mark the comment as either a suggestion or a question. All comments on the public document are hidden from other commenters during the review process. Comments on the Committee document will be visible to all other Committee members. 

STAFF REPORT – SUMMARY AND RECOMMENDATION 

Module 1 contains the zoning districts and land uses, which have been thoroughly reviewed in relation to the comprehensive plan and the current development and business contexts. The proposed land uses in Module 1B are the result of a significant rethink of how residential buildings are used and regulated. The intent is to create land use definitions that balance housing needs with the preservation of established neighborhoods as directed by the comprehensive plan. 

The substantial changes and specific questions outlined in this report are intended to highlight the significant work and guide discussion on Module 1B but are not intended to limit discussion or feedback. The intent of this module is to establish the framework of residential and institutional dwelling land uses, which will be further built upon in Module 4 when the development standards and use-specific regulations are reviewed and refined. 

RECOMMENDATION: 

Staff recommends the Rewrite Advisory Committee provide general feedback on the draft Module 1B, including direction on the specific questions listed above.

# Plano.gov/UDC 

# FEEDBACK ON MODULE 1 

Plano’s Zoning and Subdivision ordinances are being combined and updated into a single Unified Development Code document, or UDC. This rewrite aims to align the Code with our current comprehensive plan, simplify regulations, streamline the review process, and improve guidance for redevelopment. 

These ordinances are being developed in four phases, or modules. Module 1, which focuses on land uses and zoning districts, is now available for public review and feedback. The comments you provide will be shared with the Rewrite Advisory Committee, Planning & Zoning Commission, and City Council to help refine the Code before public hearings in 2026. 

# PURPOSE 

Align with the comprehensive plan 

The comprehensive plan – adopted by City Council in 2021 – is a general framework that focuses on fulfilling 

the community vision of Plano as " a global leader, excelling in exceptional education, abounding with world 

class businesses, and vibrant neighborhoods. " Many existing zoning districts will be kept to protect and 

maintain existing neighborhoods, but new zoning districts are proposed where needed to support the 

community vision and future land use map. 

Streamline, clarify, and consolidate 

The current Zoning Ordinance is a big document – 388 pages! Land use definitions and zoning districts have 

been shortened or consolidated where it makes sense, in an effort to make the Code more user-friendly. The 

draft UDC in Module 1 introduces updated zoning districts and land use definitions. Administrative standards 

and development requirements will be added to the draft UDC in later phases, and the complete draft will be 

posted for public hearings in 2026. 

# ZONING 101 

Districts 

The entire city is divided into zoning districts, which contain the rules and regulations for how property can be 

used and developed. Some properties may also be located in a second district with additional rules and 

regulations, such as a planned development or overlay district. 

Districts contain the rules for how buildings can be constructed on the property, such as the maximum building 

height and minimum distance between the building and the property lines. These rules determine the building 

form. Districts were reviewed in Module 1A. 

Land Uses 

Zoning controls how a property can be used. Every zoning district has a list of permitted uses, and every 

permitted use has a definition. The definitions are important to get right, as these determine how a business, 

home, or other activity is classified. Some uses are only permitted under certain conditions – more on that in 

Module 4, expected early 2026.

# MODULE 1B SUMMARIZED 

The current Zoning Ordinance includes many residential definitions to describe different types of buildings, but 

the activities inside the buildings are often similar or identical: cooking and eating meals, sleeping, watching 

TV, and everything else you might do at home. The UDC rethinks residential uses to separate the type of 

building from how the building is used. For example, you won’t see “Single-Family Residence Attached” in the 

use chart, but you will see residential uses which are allowed in typical townhouse developments. The building 

heights, setbacks, and density requirements for each district control where apartments, duplexes, townhouses, 

backyard cottages, and detached homes can be built. The  draft development requirements are included in 

Module 1A .

Building types 

The dwelling unit density and 

dimensional standards in the 

zoning district determine which 

building types are allowed. 

Detached  Attached  Apartment 

Residence types (This is not a complete list of all proposed residence types) 

The permitted uses in the zoning 

district determine which residence 

types are allowed. 

Private Residence  Shared Residence  Group Residence 

How does this affect me? 

In general, most of the existing homes in Plano will be re-categorized as a Private Residence or Shared 

Residence in the use table, and both uses would be permitted in every residential district. This will not change 

the type of building that is allowed. For example, apartments will only be allowed in districts where multiple 

residences are permitted on a single property, and residences in a Detached Neighborhood (RDN) zoning 

district will still need to be separated from their neighbors. 

# NEXT STEPS 

We want your feedback! 

Please review the first draft of the document and leave your comments. The comments you provide will be 

shared with the Rewrite Advisory Committee, Planning & Zoning Commission, and City Council to help refine 

the Code before public hearings in 2026.
